extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), respondents and counsel in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards used by the USPTO Administrative Law Judge to determine liability for unauthorized practice before the Office, admission by default, and appropriate sanction (including exclusion) under applicable USPTO regulations and ABA guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file answer / admission by default
rubrics_metrics.description: Part 11.36 of Title 37 of the Code of Federal Regulations states that '[f]ailure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in a default judgment.' (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent is properly served and does not file a timely answer or respond to show-cause orders, the respondent is deemed to have admitted the factual allegations and the OED Director's Default Motion may be granted; the court may issue an initial decision on default judgment. Procedural steps include service by certified mail, issuance of Notice of Hearing/Order, and Orders to Show Cause with deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized representation prohibited (35 U.S.C. § 33)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 33: 'Whoever, not being recognized to practice before the Patent and Trademark Office, holds himself out or permits himself to be held out as so recognized, or as being qualified to prepare or prosecute applications for patent, shall be fined not more than $1,000 for each offense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding oneself out as authorized to practice before the PTO when not registered is both a statutory prohibition and may support disciplinary sanctions and criminal penalties; it is an independent ground for discipline and is considered in aggravation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) states that a practitioner shall not 'engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include holding oneself out as authorized to practice before the Office when not authorized, engaging in acts or omissions that violate 35 U.S.C. § 33, providing patent legal advice without authorization, preparing a provisional application without supervision/review by a registered practitioner, and accepting compensation for unauthorized practice. Such conduct supports disciplinary sanction, including exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) states that a practitioner may not 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding oneself out as authorized to practice when not so authorized, falsely representing affiliation with a registered patent agent, and providing misleading information to clients are concrete examples of this prohibited conduct and support disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on knowingly false or misleading information to clients (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i) via §§ 10.23(a) and (b) states that a practitioner may not 'proscribe knowingly false or misleading information or knowingly participate in a material way in giving false or misleading information to a client in connection with any immediate, prospective, or pending business before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowingly false or misleading statements to clients about authorization to practice or affiliation with registered practitioners violate this provision and weigh in favor of severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceive or mislead prospective applicants (37 C.F.R. § 10.31(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation 37 C.F.R. § 10.31(a) states that a practitioner may not 'deceive or mislead any prospective applicant or other person having immediate or prospective business before the Office by word, circular, letter, or advertising, with intent to defraud in any manner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising or website statements that imply authorization or affiliation with registered patent practitioners when untrue (e.g., listing a 'contract patent agent' no longer affiliated) violate this rule and are relevant to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of competence / must associate when not competent (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(a) states that a practitioner may not 'handle a matter that the practitioner is not competent to handle without associating with another practitioner who is competent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparing patent papers or giving patent legal advice without being authorized/competent, and failing to associate or seek assistance from a registered patent practitioner (including failing to obtain supervision or review of a provisional application) violates this rule and supports sanctions for incompetence/unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct that adversely reflects on a practitioner's fitness (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) states that a practitioner may not 'proscribe or engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on a practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts and omissions not otherwise falling under specific counts but that undermine a practitioner's fitness (e.g., neglect, noncommunication, misrepresentations) can be charged under this provision and affect sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing patent legal advice / preparing filings while unauthorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing patent legal advice, preparing a provisional patent application, or otherwise performing patent services when not authorized to practice before the USPTO constitutes unauthorized practice and a rule violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific factual examples include preparing a provisional application without supervision or review by a registered practitioner, neglecting to file the application, and giving incorrect patent-filing advice (e.g., incorrect statements about obtaining a filing date by mailing). Such acts support findings of misconduct and justify sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting compensation for unauthorized practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting payment or compensation for performing patent legal services while not authorized to practice before the USPTO is prohibited and constitutes misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipt of fees for unauthorized patent services is an aggravating fact supporting exclusion or other sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-factor sanctioning analysis (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions such as exclusion, the Court must consider four factors: (1) did the practitioner violate a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) did the practitioner act intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) what amount of actual or potential injury was caused; and (4) are there any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each factor is assessed to determine appropriate discipline; the decision applies these by finding duties violated (failure to inform clients, neglect), state of mind (knowing/negligent, knowledge may be inferred), potential injury (foreseeable harm from delay), and aggravation/mitigation (e.g., criminality as aggravating; burden on respondent to prove mitigation). The combination of these factors can support maximal sanctions including exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of mind standard / inference of knowledge (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 11.1, 'knowing' means actual knowledge of the fact in question, and knowledge may be inferred from circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In default cases, the respondent's failure to appear can result in waiver of contesting state of mind; the court may infer willfulness or actual knowledge from surrounding facts and circumstances when assessing culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual or potential injury standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions consider the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; a 'potential injury' is a harm that is 'reasonably foreseeable at the time of the lawyer's misconduct' (citing ABA Standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays in filing patent applications or failures to communicate can cause foreseeable potential injury to clients' intellectual property rights and thus support harsher sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors — illegal or criminal conduct (ABA Standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court looks to the American Bar Association Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions; illegal conduct (e.g., violations of criminal law such as unauthorized representation under 35 U.S.C. § 33) is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of illegal conduct supports a maximum sanction; the decision explicitly cites the ABA Standards and treats false representations as illegal conduct constituting aggravation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors and burden to raise them
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating circumstances must be affirmatively raised by the respondent and shown to have nexus to the misconduct (citing 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.36(c) and 11.49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In default, failure to respond means the respondent has not presented mitigating evidence; absence of mitigation supports harsher sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural service and notice requirements for disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper service (e.g., mailing complaint by certified mail with return receipt requested), issuance of Notices of Hearing, Orders to Show Cause with deadlines, and opportunities to answer or respond are required procedural steps before default judgment may be entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation of service and adherence to deadlines is necessary to support a default decision; the decision details service dates, attempts to contact respondent, and issuance of show-cause orders before granting default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.55, any appeal from the Initial Decision must be filed with the USPTO within 30 days after the date of the Initial Decision and must include exceptions to the Administrative Law Judge's decision and supporting reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file an appeal in accordance with § 11.55 will be deemed acceptance of the Initial Decision and waiver of rights to further administrative and judicial review. The appeal must be filed at the address provided in 37 C.F.R. § 1.1(a)(3)(ii).
